# Other International News
* **U.S. strike on boat in Pacific kills five people:** The U.S. military attacked what it [said](https://substack.com/redirect/036b94c8-1431-465a-97b2-3246096c084a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) was a drug-smuggling boat in the eastern Pacific on Tuesday, killing five people. U.S. Southern Command claimed that "intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narcotrafficking," without providing any evidence underlying the intelligence. It published a [video on X](https://substack.com/redirect/0f14d12e-d9dc-4268-a6c1-29f417631d66?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that shows a small boat enveloped by an explosion. Since the U.S. military began targeting what it calls "narcoterrorists" in September 2025, it has killed more than 240 people in more than 70 attacks.
* **Fl avio Bolsonaro and family flee Brazil; U.S. to provide visas:** The United States will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family, the State Department [said](https://substack.com/redirect/83d9eb2e-604a-49c0-9531-47d6ab2d74a9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) on Tuesday. Bolsonaro arrived in Miami on Wednesday morning, according to news reports. After losing the presidential election to the incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, police requested that Bolsonaro turn over his Brazilian and diplomatic passports. He has been under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering.
* **Toll from Sudanese military strike on exceeds 100 deaths, rights group says:** The death toll from a Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) attack on a busy market in Nyala, South Darfur, [rose](https://substack.com/redirect/05da66cd-4667-4763-a8f3-c1b09d688345?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to more than 100 deaths and 113 injuries, the rights group Emergency Lawyers said on Tuesday. Many of the victims were women and children. The SAF attacked the market on Monday evening.
* Separately, a drone strike on the Al-Markhiyat transformer station in Omdurman, which an official from the state-run Sudanese Electricity Distribution Company blamed on the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), left large swaths of Khartoum without power for over 12 hours. Approximately 60% of the capital's electrical supply was affected by the strike, forcing hospitals and bakeries to rely on back-up generators.
* **Strikes on Sudan gold mines kill five:** Drone strikes, likely carried out by the RSF, [killed](https://substack.com/redirect/4ae60f5a-3e1e-494a-9b5c-bc39be36d370?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) at least five people and injured several others at several artisanal mining sites in South Kordofan, Sudan, on Tuesday. The RSF has previously targeted South Kordofan mining areas. Artisanal mining, which is done under exacting conditions, employs more than two million people in Sudan and produces over 80% of the country's gold.
* **Mada Masr chief editor released, faces another trial:** Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was released on Tuesday evening after paying a 3 million Egyptian pound fine ordered by a Cairo court that convicted her of running a news outlet without a license. The court also ordered the closure of Mada Masr and the seizure of its assets.
* On Wednesday, the outlet said in its newsletter: "Mada Masr is still considering its legal position following the conviction. As of yet, we don't know where things stand, when you will hear from us next, or what we will say."
* During release procedures, Attalah was informed for the first time that another court had sentenced her in absentia in 2024 to one year in prison on charges of publishing false news and managing an unlicensed website. Her lawyers have challenged that sentence. A retrial is scheduled for November 11.
* Over 120 rights organizations and independent media outlets, including Drop Site News, signed a [joint statement](https://substack.com/redirect/5cc03e55-ca19-4d25-907a-75a21f043af4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) condemning the conviction and calling on Egyptian authorities to allow Mada Masr to operate freely. In Congress, Rep. Don Beyer [described](https://substack.com/redirect/cfae2c29-21dc-48aa-91df-5b5225ebeeb2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) the conviction as "a massive escalation" of Egyptian authorities' "crackdown on independent media," and "a brazen attack on press freedom and an attempt to silence one of the last major independent voices in Egypt."
* **Syria-Jordan border reopens amid probe into deadly strikes:** Syria [reopened](https://substack.com/redirect/50598a36-2afe-4fa0-853f-aa3e6a3c7ab2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) the Nassib crossing, Jordan's only border crossing with Syria, on Wednesday morning, with regular passenger and commercial traffic resuming, SANA reported. The crossing had briefly closed after Jordanian strikes on suspected ISIS hideouts in southern Syria on Monday, which killed at least seven people in Deraa and Suweyda. Jordan launched the attacks in response to a church shooting in Karak on Friday, for which ISIS claimed responsibility, that killed at least nine people and wounded 34 others.
* Also on Tuesday, the two countries' foreign ministers agreed in a phone call to form a security committee to review the incidents and improve intelligence coordination. During the call, Jordan's Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi expressed "deep regret" over civilian deaths that occurred as a result of Monday's Jordanian strikes.
* **Nigeria says 37 jailed miners died in their cells from overcrowding and neglect:** Thirty-seven miners, who were jailed on charges of illegal mining, died in detention last month. A Nigerian government investigation [found](https://substack.com/redirect/87dec922-41e9-4fd8-aacd-d73d1182a7f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that the deaths were the result of severe overcrowding and poor ventilation. The detainees also suffered from heat stress and dehydration, the report noted. The chairman of the investigation, Jonathan Kure, called the deaths "entirely preventable." Last month, witnesses in the detention facility [told](https://substack.com/redirect/2d70232b-5240-49cd-a957-f868ded09403?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) Reuters that prison guards "sprayed an unidentified substance into a crowded cell where dozens of detainees died and kept the doors locked, ignoring cries for help."
* The government panel overseeing the investigation recommended that each victim's family receive 30 million naira (about $22,500), and that each of the 41 survivors receive 10 million naira. The panel advised a sweeping overhaul of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps, which detained the miners.
* **Dozens of Somali soldiers killed in major al-Shabaab battle:** Dozens of Somali troops [died](https://substack.com/redirect/16a2a1ab-70f7-4dd5-afc0-2f7ee9f2fbc3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in fighting against al-Shabaab Islamist insurgents in the Buurhakaba district of southern Somalia, Reuters reported on Tuesday. One soldier said that he helped carry 40 dead soldiers and over 100 wounded others to hospitals in Mogadishu. Another said that al-Shabaab deployed car bombs that wrecked five military vehicles. Government forces killed about 75 militants and wounded 56, the Defense Ministry said, adding that al-Shabaab militants used explosives-packed vehicles in their attacks. Somalia has fought al-Shabaab militants for nearly two decades.
* **Tanzania 's jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu ends hunger strike: **Tundu Lissu, who [leads](https://substack.com/redirect/5e2dddb1-983c-4da6-ba0b-3496c91ec2b9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) the Tanzanian opposition party CHADEMA and came in second place in the 2020 presidential election, ended a brief hunger strike after prison authorities allowed him to meet privately with his lawyers on Tuesday. He began the strike on either Monday or Tuesday. Tanzania's prison service denied that he went on hunger strike at all. Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason over a speech that prosecutors said urged the public to rebel and disrupt the 2025 election. Violence following that election led to the deaths of at least 518 people. Lissu pleaded not guilty, calling the case political. A judgment in his case is due in early November.
* **El Salvador rushes about 1,000 troops to Haiti after gang ambush:** El Salvador has sent about 1,000 troops to Haiti since an October 18 gang ambush near Port-au-Prince that led to the disappearance of four Salvadoran soldiers with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, Reuters [reported](https://substack.com/redirect/82e3c3e9-aec9-4304-95ae-9adaf7a37ed1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). It is unclear who will command the new deployment, how long the troops will remain on the ground, or whether more will follow. The U.S. provided C-130 aircraft to move the troops. The UN-backed force comprises about 2,000 personnel. Gangs have internally displaced almost 1.5 million people in Haiti.
* **Spain deports migrants from Ceuta in move criticized by Amnesty:** Spain deported migrants from Ceuta after their asylum applications were rejected and Morocco agreed to take them, Spain's Interior Ministry [said](https://substack.com/redirect/d3eefcbc-030d-4b1a-8e71-223e2f5afd1d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) Tuesday. These are the first deportations of their kind since a mass crossing of migrants from Morocco to Ceuta in July. NGOs told Reuters that 16 people were deported; they hail from African, Middle Eastern, and Asian countries. Amnesty International criticized the Spanish government, warning that the human rights of deportees could be at risk. About 80,000 people entered Ceuta over 48 hours in July; at least 100 died swimming around marine barriers or in stampedes and about 8,000 migrants remain, some of whom are sleeping on the streets.
* **Iraq PM sacks intelligence chief and advisers:** Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi [fired](https://substack.com/redirect/5d12a075-615c-42e1-ba75-a69bdd491c45?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) the head of the National Intelligence Service, Hamid al-Shatri, a post he held since December 2024. No reason for the firing was given, and al-Shatri's successor has not been named, public broadcaster Iraqi News Agency reported. Through an official, the prime minister announced a campaign against "public-sector overstaffing." He terminated the contracts of 69 advisers and staff in his office.

International Atomic Energy Agency says no evidence Iran has rebuilt nuclear facilities damaged in U.S.-Israeli strikes. Gulf states reportedly push diplomatic deal involving Iran, Yemen, and Hormuz. Netanyahu falls short of majority; no clear winner in Israeli elections. Yemen : Ansarallah missile hits Aden airport. Ansarallah-appointed governor claims most of Yemen's Taiz is under its control. UN Ambassador Mike Waltz and Cuban Foreign Minister argue on UN floor. President Donald Trump again calls for Venezuela to be 51st state. State Department official Jeremy Lewin leaves post ahead of midterms. Grand jury declines to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson. This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday - Friday Iran Qatar presents new proposal to end Iran war: Qatari mediators Iran with a new seven-day proposal to end the eight-month U.S.-Israeli war. A senior Iranian official said the proposal consisted of "unacceptable ideas" and that it was "not an offer," according to Reuters. The proposal, reportedly approved by the U.S., outlined daily confidence-building measures by both sides, potentially beginning early next week, with several countries serving as guarantors, according to an official briefed on the negotiations. Qatari mediators presented it to Iran on Sunday, the official added. Washington insists that nuclear negotiations begin immediately, while Iran demands an end to the U.S. blockade and the lifting of oil sanctions before beginning those negotiations. The diplomatic push comes amid renewed threats of military escalation. The U.S. several Gulf Arab states to prepare for a "short, intense military campaign" following next week's U.S. midterm elections, according to the Wall Street Journal. Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi that the "devastating impact on international markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure" in the Persian Gulf remains a major concern for global energy producers and consumers. Iran denies involvement in alleged assassination plot in Kuwait after three sentenced to death: Iran's embassy in Kuwait accusations that an Iranian national was involved in a plot to assassinate senior Kuwaiti officials, saying on Wednesday that the individual had not been in Kuwait for the past decade. The statement came after a Kuwaiti court sentenced three defendants to death on Monday, including Iranian national Abdulreza Dehqani, and two Kuwaiti nationals, while eight others received five-year prison sentences. Kuwaiti prosecutors accused the defendants of espionage for Iran and Lebanon's Hezbollah and of plotting to assassinate the First Deputy Prime Minister, the Interior Minister, and other senior officials. U.S. military spending on Iran war surpasses $47 billion, up more than 25% since July: The U.S. military has more than $47 billion on its war against Iran, over 25% higher than the Pentagon's $37.5 billion estimate in July, according to internal War Department figures obtained by Reuters. The latest estimate includes more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions and over $6 billion to replace lost military equipment, including aircraft and drones. The figures do not clearly account for the potentially enormous cost of repairing U.S. military bases damaged by Iranian missile and drone attacks. IAEA says no evidence Iran has rebuilt nuclear facilities damaged in U.S.-Israeli strikes: The head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) that there was no activity suggesting Iran has attempted to repair or rebuild nuclear facilities damaged by U.S. and Israeli attacks in 2025 and 2026. "Since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026," Director General Rafael Grossi told the UN Security Council on Tuesday. But he stressed that the agency still needs access to verify the facilities' condition and account for previously declared nuclear material, including 440 kilograms of highly enriched uranium. Gulf states reportedly push diplomatic deal involving Iran, Yemen, and Hormuz: Gulf states are a diplomatic deal to avert another U.S.-Iran war that involves the Strait of Hormuz, Yemen, and a new regional security framework, The Guardian reported. Iran's Mohsen Rezaei met Ansarallah's ambassador a day after senior Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani officials visited Tehran. Iran could sway Ansarallah, potentially facilitating a settlement short of total military victory--expelling Saudi Arabia from the country. Ansarallah is demanding an end to Saudi Arabia's air and naval blockade. According to The Guardian, Iran "successfully prevented discussion of its nuclear programme" at the Tehran meeting, instead steering talks toward a regional security arrangement that would include Iran and Gulf states while reducing or ending the U.S. military presence in the Middle East. UAE closes all Sharjah beaches as tanker oil spill spreads across northern emirates: Authorities in Sharjah closed all beaches across the city following an oil spill from a damaged tanker in nearby waters, describing the decision as a "proactive precautionary measure." The closure comes after dozens of beaches and coastal areas across Umm Al Quwain and Ras Al Khaimah have been shut down in recent days, with satellite imagery showing the spill stretching across the UAE's northern coastline. Experts told Reuters the oil was leaking from the Panama-flagged Gem No. 2, a tanker reportedly struck by an unidentified projectile last month. Palestine Four Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes across Gaza: An** Israeli on the Mawasi area of Rafah, southern Gaza, killed three Palestinians and wounded at least 10 on Wednesday, according to WAFA. A drone strike in the Mawasi area of Al-Qarara, north of Khan Younis, southern Gaza, killed one Palestinian and wounded several others. Separately, a Palestinian man and his daughter were wounded in an Israeli strike on the Ard Al-Laymoun area south of Khan Younis. Over the past 24 hours, Israeli attacks killed three Palestinians--one in a new Israeli attack and two after succumbing to wounds sustained in earlier attacks--and injured 11 others across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023, is now 74,564 killed, with 175,770 injured. Since October 11, 2025, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,568 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 5,649, while 845 bodies have been recovered. Israeli forces demolish homes in the occupied West Bank as Hebron assault enters sixth day: Hebron: Israeli forces their military assault for the sixth consecutive day on Wednesday, sealing off the neighborhoods of Al-Jalda and Deir Baha, raiding homes, destroying property, and converting residential buildings into military outposts, WAFA reported. Around 780 families have been affected by the siege, with nearly 5,000 Palestinians forcibly displaced or confined to their homes, according to Hebron Municipality. Israeli forces detained approximately 110 Palestinians, including seven children and three women, and subjected hundreds more to field interrogations, according to the Palestinian Prisoners Society. Nablus: Israeli forces one home and blew up another in Beita after forcing residents to evacuate the western part of the town. In Yasid, north of Nablus, Israeli soldiers beat a Palestinian and his son during a raid, leaving one with a fractured hand. Bethlehem: Israeli forces road closures across the governorate for the sixth consecutive day, blocking access to several towns and villages. Tulkarm: Israeli forces four Palestinians, including the journalist and former prisoner Hamza Salama and two of his brothers. An officer in the Palestinian General Intelligence Service, Mohammed Al-Qass, was arrested during a raid on his home. Workers at nearly 50 ports worldwide plan Friday strikes in solidarity with Gaza : Trade unions at nearly 50 ports worldwide, spanning Mexico, Europe, and India, are strikes and demonstrations on Friday in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza, demanding an end to Israel's genocide and unrestricted humanitarian aid access, according to Shaher Saad, secretary-general of the Palestinian General Federation of Trade Unions. The actions are being coordinated with the International Transport Workers' Federation. Netanyahu falls short of majority; no clear winner in Israeli elections: Neither of the two leading political camps have yet secured the 61 seats required to win a parliamentary majority in the 120-member Knesset. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc has secured 53 seats. Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot's bloc stands at 48 seats. As of 12:34 p.m. local time on Wednesday, 84.5% of ballots were counted, according to preliminary results. Palestinian parties are projected to secure 19 seats. Although they have significant leverage given their electoral gains, it is unclear if any opposition bloc would be willing to form a coalition with them to form a majority. Netanyahu openly dismissed the idea, saying, "We must not endanger Israel and establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties." Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump claimed that his endorsement of Netanyahu "helped him a lot." "It's looking like maybe a stalemate or a win," Trump told reporters. Yemen Ansarallah missile hits Aden airport: An Ansarallah missile reportedly hit Aden International Airport in southern Yemen on Wednesday. Ansarallah military spokesperson Yahya Saree called for the immediate evacuation of the airport, claiming that a Saudi military cargo plane was transporting weapons intended for use against Yemenis. The group later repeated the , describing it as its "final" call for everyone at the airport to leave immediately. The missile reportedly struck the airport before the group issued its warnings, according to a police source cited by AFP. Ansarallah-appointed governor claims most of Yemen 's Taiz is under its control: The province of Taiz is under the control of Ansarallah, except for parts of Taiz city, the Ansarallah-appointed governor of Taiz Ahmed Al-Masawa Tuesday in an interview with Ansarallah's Al-Masirah TV. Taiz city, the provincial capital, is still under siege and largely controlled by Saudi-backed government forces. Human Rights Watch that roads into and out of Taiz city have been "largely blocked by government-affiliated and Houthi forces" since October 1. It also documents Ansarallah forces blowing up the Hayjat Al-Abd road on October 18, the main entry point for food, medicine and fuel. Lebanon Israeli forces bombard southern Lebanon towns amid "ceasefire": Nabatieh: Israeli artillery shelling the area between Mifdoun and Zawtar Al-Sharqieh on Wednesday morning, Lebanon's National News Agency reported. Tyre (Sour): Israeli artillery shelled Mansouri, Majdal Zoun, and surrounding valleys. Marjeyoun: Israeli forces two large explosions, one near the cemetery in Khiam and another in the town of Tallouseh on Tuesday. U.S. News Man dies in ICE facility in San Diego, the 30th death in ICE detention this year: Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez , a detainee at ICE's Otay Mesa facility in San Diego, at the facility on Saturday, ICE said on Monday. Gutierrez, a 43-year-old Guatemalan national, was arrested in Escondido and had been in custody since October 9. ICE said that he was in an "assigned safety cell" at the Core Civic-run facility when he died. The agency also claimed that Gutierrez was detained in July 2024 after being convicted of selling liquor to a minor and several other arrests without apparent convictions. The local news outlet Daylight San Diego could not locate court records matching ICE's claims. ICE said that a judge ordered him deported to Mexico in 2006. Ambassador Waltz and Cuban Foreign Minister argue on UN floor: U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz with Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodr iguez Parrilla on Tuesday, after Waltz delivered an inflammatory speech criticizing the Cuban government. Rodriguez Parrilla approached the podium during the speech, and Waltz told him to back up, saying that Rodriguez was trying to "intimidate me in the United States of America like he tries to intimidate political prisoners" in Cuba. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman requested that Waltz be allowed to finish his speech before hearing Cuba's point of order. Decorum continued to break down, and Rahman suspended the meeting. Trump again calls for Venezuela to be 51st state: At an event in Texas on Tuesday, Trump that Venezuela should be made part of the United States. "Maybe someday soon, it will become a prosperous 51st state," he said, adding that "instead of a president, we'll have an election for a governor." Addressing the oil tycoon Harold Hamm , who was in the crowd, he said, "Let's make it the 51st state." Earlier this year, Trump said that he was "seriously considering" making Venezuela a state. The country's acting president, Delcy Rodr iguez, said in May that Venezuela had no plans to become a U.S. state and that it would defend its sovereignty. Rubio adviser Jeremy Lewin leaves State Department ahead of midterms: Jeremy Lewin , the 29-year-old under secretary and director of policy planning at the State Department, on Tuesday that he was leaving the administration for a job in the private sector. Lewin, a DOGE alum who helped dismantle USAID, led U.S. engagement with Venezuela's Delcy Rodr iguez, helped assemble Trump's Venezuela oil deal, and led bilateral talks in Havana with Ra ul Guillermo Rodriguez Castro, grandson of Ra ul Castro. Separately on Tuesday, WIRED reported on Lewin's time at USAID, where for three weeks Lewin essentially ran the agency as if he was its director, canceling lifesaving aid programs and dismissing employees even though he had not signed the paperwork required to work at the agency. The full report from WIRED is available . Grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson: A federal grand jury in Washington on Tuesday a "no true bill" on the Justice Department's bid to indict Cassidy Hutchinson , the former White House aide who testified against the administration to Congress regarding the January 6 Capitol attack. The DOJ tried to charge Hutchinson with lying to Congress, the New York Times reported. Some DOJ prosecutors were reportedly skeptical of the case, which was led by Trump loyalist Harmeet Dhillon , head of the department's civil rights division. FBI raids billionaire Stephen Cloobeck 's Beverly Hills mansion in connection with Eric Swalwell probe: FBI agents a sealed search warrant on Tuesday at the Beverly Hills home of Stephen Cloobeck , billionaire owner of the timeshare company Diamond Resorts. Eric Swalwell stayed at the home several times while campaigning, an FBI spokesperson said. Swalwell dropped out of the California governor's race and resigned from Congress in April after allegations that he sexually assaulted a former staffer and acted inappropriately with other young women, which he denied. In August, federal agents seized Swalwell's devices, raided his Washington home, and briefly held him at San Francisco International Airport. Earlier in the summer, they searched his Dublin home. Separately, authorities in New York and Los Angeles County are investigating the ex-congressman. Hackers target FEC system, disrupting campaign finance filings a week before midterms: The Federal Elections Commission on Tuesday that its electronic filing system has been offline since Monday evening, forcing a shutdown of web-facing services. An FEC filings officer told compliance firms that "we have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems," according to an email seen by Reuters. The outage blocks 24- and 48-hour spending reports, though past reports remain searchable and voters' ability to cast ballots is unaffected. Hasan Piker sues Scott Jennings for defamation over edited lynching clip: The leftist Twitch streamer Hasan Piker a federal suit in Washington, DC, on Tuesday, alleging that the conservative commentator Scott Jennings aired manipulated footage of him. According to the 38-page filing, an August 11 episode of "The Scott Jennings Show" included footage of Piker that contained misleading quotations. Captions attributed to Piker the line "Let's go back to a better time when lynchings were happening." Jennings then accused him of "calling for Black voters to be lynched." Jennings posted the edited segment on X, and tied Piker to the Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Jennings described Piker as El-Sayed's "best pal and campaign partner." The X post drew about 2.5 million views. Piker's suit said that Jennings refused to retract the post after receiving a written demand on August 31, and that Jennings harmed Piker's reputation and his income from streaming, advertising, and sponsorship deals. Trump moves to loosen rules for oil and gas firms: On Tuesday, President Trump an Environmental Protection Agency plan to weaken federal rules governing methane emissions, calling the Biden-era rules "expensive and unnecessary." The proposal would relax EPA requirements for hundreds of thousands of low-output "marginal" wells, end the agency's Methane Super Emitter Program, and reverse a rule requiring operators to capture the additional gas that leaks from wells. Although "marginal" wells make up about 7% of U.S. oil and gas production, they account for roughly half of the industry's methane emissions. Supreme Court lets Texas-Justice Department deal on deportation proceedings stand: On Tuesday, the Supreme Court to block an agreement ending immigration judges' discretion to suspend deportation cases through "administrative closure." The procedural tool allows judges to halt deportation proceedings under certain circumstances, such as when an immigrant seeks humanitarian protection to remain in the U.S. The plaintiffs in the case, several U.S. cities and the advocacy group Centro Legal, argued in favor of the legitimacy of administrative closure. NYPD cancels no-bid contract with Israeli surveillance firm: The New York Police Department will not pursue a "sole source procurement" deal with the Israeli firm Cognyte for AI-driven surveillance technology, an NYPD spokesperson on Tuesday. According to the spokesperson, the firm "did not meet the criteria" for such an arrangement and that the NYPD would conduct "an open, competitive procurement process." The decision comes after allies of Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized the contract. The Israeli firm's FalcoNet technology would allow police to intercept cell-phone communications. Similar technology is already used by the department, though experts say that the FalcoNet system would significantly increase police surveillance capacities. 📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill? Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com Other International News U.S. strike on boat in Pacific kills five people: The U.S. military attacked what it was a drug-smuggling boat in the eastern Pacific on Tuesday, killing five people. U.S. Southern Command claimed that "intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narcotrafficking," without providing any evidence underlying the intelligence. It published a that shows a small boat enveloped by an explosion. Since the U.S. military began targeting what it calls "narcoterrorists" in September 2025, it has killed more than 240 people in more than 70 attacks. Fl avio Bolsonaro and family flee Brazil; U.S. to provide visas: The United States will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family, the State Department on Tuesday. Bolsonaro arrived in Miami on Wednesday morning, according to news reports. After losing the presidential election to the incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, police requested that Bolsonaro turn over his Brazilian and diplomatic passports. He has been under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering. Toll from Sudanese military strike on exceeds 100 deaths, rights group says: The death toll from a Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) attack on a busy market in Nyala, South Darfur, to more than 100 deaths and 113 injuries, the rights group Emergency Lawyers said on Tuesday. Many of the victims were women and children. The SAF attacked the market on Monday evening. Separately, a drone strike on the Al-Markhiyat transformer station in Omdurman, which an official from the state-run Sudanese Electricity Distribution Company blamed on the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), left large swaths of Khartoum without power for over 12 hours. Approximately 60% of the capital's electrical supply was affected by the strike, forcing hospitals and bakeries to rely on back-up generators. Strikes on Sudan gold mines kill five: Drone strikes, likely carried out by the RSF, at least five people and injured several others at several artisanal mining sites in South Kordofan, Sudan, on Tuesday. The RSF has previously targeted South Kordofan mining areas. Artisanal mining, which is done under exacting conditions, employs more than two million people in Sudan and produces over 80% of the country's gold. Mada Masr chief editor released, faces another trial: Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was released on Tuesday evening after paying a 3 million Egyptian pound fine ordered by a Cairo court that convicted her of running a news outlet without a license. The court also ordered the closure of Mada Masr and the seizure of its assets. On Wednesday, the outlet said in its newsletter: "Mada Masr is still considering its legal position following the conviction. As of yet, we don't know where things stand, when you will hear from us next, or what we will say." During release procedures, Attalah was informed for the first time that another court had sentenced her in absentia in 2024 to one year in prison on charges of publishing false news and managing an unlicensed website. Her lawyers have challenged that sentence. A retrial is scheduled for November 11. Over 120 rights organizations and independent media outlets, including Drop Site News, signed a condemning the conviction and calling on Egyptian authorities to allow Mada Masr to operate freely. In Congress, Rep. Don Beyer the conviction as "a massive escalation" of Egyptian authorities' "crackdown on independent media," and "a brazen attack on press freedom and an attempt to silence one of the last major independent voices in Egypt." Syria-Jordan border reopens amid probe into deadly strikes: Syria the Nassib crossing, Jordan's only border crossing with Syria, on Wednesday morning, with regular passenger and commercial traffic resuming, SANA reported. The crossing had briefly closed after Jordanian strikes on suspected ISIS hideouts in southern Syria on Monday, which killed at least seven people in Deraa and Suweyda. Jordan launched the attacks in response to a church shooting in Karak on Friday, for which ISIS claimed responsibility, that killed at least nine people and wounded 34 others. Also on Tuesday, the two countries' foreign ministers agreed in a phone call to form a security committee to review the incidents and improve intelligence coordination. During the call, Jordan's Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi expressed "deep regret" over civilian deaths that occurred as a result of Monday's Jordanian strikes. Nigeria says 37 jailed miners died in their cells from overcrowding and neglect: Thirty-seven miners, who were jailed on charges of illegal mining, died in detention last month. A Nigerian government investigation that the deaths were the result of severe overcrowding and poor ventilation. The detainees also suffered from heat stress and dehydration, the report noted. The chairman of the investigation, Jonathan Kure, called the deaths "entirely preventable." Last month, witnesses in the detention facility Reuters that prison guards "sprayed an unidentified substance into a crowded cell where dozens of detainees died and kept the doors locked, ignoring cries for help." The government panel overseeing the investigation recommended that each victim's family receive 30 million naira (about $22,500), and that each of the 41 survivors receive 10 million naira. The panel advised a sweeping overhaul of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps, which detained the miners. Dozens of Somali soldiers killed in major al-Shabaab battle: Dozens of Somali troops in fighting against al-Shabaab Islamist insurgents in the Buurhakaba district of southern Somalia, Reuters reported on Tuesday. One soldier said that he helped carry 40 dead soldiers and over 100 wounded others to hospitals in Mogadishu. Another said that al-Shabaab deployed car bombs that wrecked five military vehicles. Government forces killed about 75 militants and wounded 56, the Defense Ministry said, adding that al-Shabaab militants used explosives-packed vehicles in their attacks. Somalia has fought al-Shabaab militants for nearly two decades. Tanzania 's jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu ends hunger strike: Tundu Lissu, who the Tanzanian opposition party CHADEMA and came in second place in the 2020 presidential election, ended a brief hunger strike after prison authorities allowed him to meet privately with his lawyers on Tuesday. He began the strike on either Monday or Tuesday. Tanzania's prison service denied that he went on hunger strike at all. Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason over a speech that prosecutors said urged the public to rebel and disrupt the 2025 election. Violence following that election led to the deaths of at least 518 people. Lissu pleaded not guilty, calling the case political. A judgment in his case is due in early November. El Salvador rushes about 1,000 troops to Haiti after gang ambush: El Salvador has sent about 1,000 troops to Haiti since an October 18 gang ambush near Port-au-Prince that led to the disappearance of four Salvadoran soldiers with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, Reuters . It is unclear who will command the new deployment, how long the troops will remain on the ground, or whether more will follow. The U.S. provided C-130 aircraft to move the troops. The UN-backed force comprises about 2,000 personnel. Gangs have internally displaced almost 1.5 million people in Haiti. Spain deports migrants from Ceuta in move criticized by Amnesty: Spain deported migrants from Ceuta after their asylum applications were rejected and Morocco agreed to take them, Spain's Interior Ministry Tuesday. These are the first deportations of their kind since a mass crossing of migrants from Morocco to Ceuta in July. NGOs told Reuters that 16 people were deported; they hail from African, Middle Eastern, and Asian countries. Amnesty International criticized the Spanish government, warning that the human rights of deportees could be at risk. About 80,000 people entered Ceuta over 48 hours in July; at least 100 died swimming around marine barriers or in stampedes and about 8,000 migrants remain, some of whom are sleeping on the streets. Iraq PM sacks intelligence chief and advisers: Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi the head of the National Intelligence Service, Hamid al-Shatri, a post he held since December 2024. No reason for the firing was given, and al-Shatri's successor has not been named, public broadcaster Iraqi News Agency reported. Through an official, the prime minister announced a campaign against "public-sector overstaffing." Friends,
This Friday, October 30, I'll be participating in a special three-hour live broadcast of **BBC Newshour** , focused primarily on Pennsylvania's midterm elections and what our Commonwealth may tell us about the political direction of the rest of the nation.
_**And I have a personal invitation for you.**_
**Come out and show your support!**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b74b8300-9101-4222-a32a-d1f05d2471cb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Pennsylvania has long been considered a political bellwether. From Philadelphia to Pittsburgh, from our suburbs to our rural communities, Pennsylvania is a fascinating reflection of the political, economic, and cultural debates taking place across America.
And this Friday, BBC Newshour is coming to Harrisburg to explore those very questions.
**What is happening in Pennsylvania? What are voters thinking? And what might it tell us about the rest of the country?**
Now, I don't think anyone would mistake the BBC for a conservative news organization.
And that's precisely why I welcome this opportunity.
It's easy to have conversations with people who already agree with us. It's something altogether different to walk into a room where our ideas may be challenged, our convictions questioned, and our perspective isn't necessarily the prevailing one.
But isn't that exactly where we should be?
**We have to show up. We have to be prepared. And we have to make our case.**
### And here's where YOU come in.
BBC Newshour will broadcast live from the beautiful Midtown Scholar Bookstore in Harrisburg, with the program reaching listeners through the BBC World Service and Pennsylvania public radio stations, including WHYY, WITF, and WVIA.
I would love to look out into that audience and see familiar faces.
Friends. Supporters. People who understand that showing up matters, especially when the conversation extends beyond our own communities.
Your presence would mean a great deal to me.
Not because I need everyone in the room to agree with me, but because I believe in the value of showing up, engaging in thoughtful disagreement, and participating in conversations that help shape how our state and country are understood.
And, frankly, **it would just be wonderful to see some friendly faces in the room!**
### Come show your support!
**Friday, October 30, 2026**
**Time:** 3:00 PM - 6:00 PM
**Location:** Midtown Scholar Bookstore
1302 North Third Street
Harrisburg, PA 17102
**Program:** BBC Newshour -- Special Live Pennsylvania Midterm Election Coverage
Come experience a live international news broadcast. Bring a friend. And join us as Pennsylvania takes center stage in a conversation about America's political future.
**We don 't need every microphone to agree with us. We just need the courage to speak when one is offered.**
I hope to see you Friday!
Blessings,
**Kathy Barnette**
_P.S. If you 're anywhere within driving distance of Harrisburg, I'd love for you to make the trip. Three hours of live radio, a conversation about Pennsylvania's political future, and an opportunity to be part of the audience. Come join us!_

Goldwater lost forty-four states in 1964 and the right called it a down payment: run the argument, lose the night, keep the philosophy, win later. Ronald Reagan cut his teeth delivering "A Time for Choosing." The Grahams put evangelical muscle behind the fights for the unborn and the classroom, and Franklin Graham prayed the champion into office in January 2017. Pat Buchanan climbed a Houston stage in August 1992 and named it in daylight -- "a religious war going on in our country for the soul of America" -- and the hall roared, grateful somebody finally would. Ann Coulter shipped the paperback editions, footnotes included, and made "amnesty" a word no Republican dared touch in a primary.
For sixty years, the party's product was the fight itself: against bloat, against open borders, against judges who legislate, against budgets that never balance. Then, in 2016, the fight finally got a champion who won.
Ten years on, it is fair to ask what the champion did with the war he was handed. The answer is a surrender -- not signed, but conducted line by line, carve-out by carve-out. The pledges still hang on the wall. The policy lives in the fine print. MAGA didn't lose the culture wars. It cashed them out...

subject: Ungodly sums of money in Texas
body:
[1]Talarico for Texas

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261028-2-subs-a&t=1001&akid=1158%2E1347274%2Et5SqAR ]John Grisham

Peter —

It’s John Grisham. I’m reaching out because I believe James Talarico
deserves your support.

But first, I want to tell you a story. Almost twenty years ago, I wrote a
book called The Appeal. It’s about how one wealthy, powerful man uses his
money to bankroll a campaign and install a puppet politician in office.

Rather than face accountability in court, the man rigs the system to
guarantee the outcome he wants. It works so well that the politician is
willing to betray his own family at the wealthy donor’s behest.

This was years before Citizens United, at a time when I couldn’t fathom
how obscenely expensive and corrupt our elections would become today.
What’s happening right now in Texas is a version of that story on
steroids.

In Texas’ Senate race, Elon Musk — the richest man in the world — is
openly spending nearly two hundred million dollars to install the most
corrupt politician in Texas in the U.S. Senate.

And Ken Paxton isn’t waiting to do Musk’s bidding. He’s already using his
position as Attorney General to push Elon Musk’s data center agenda and
investigate Musk’s corporate rivals.

It couldn’t be a starker contrast with James Talarico, who his running to
take on corruption and get the ungodly sums of money out of our politics.
I truly believe sending James to the U.S. Senate can create the political
earthquake necessary to change our broken system.

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261028-2-subs-a&t=1002&akid=1158%2E1347274%2Et5SqAR ]If you can, please consider making a contribution to his campaign to

Dream In the go-big-or-go-home collective consciousness of Texas, no
ambition is deemed too reckless, no daydream too wild. Save perhaps one.
It is the idea, fantastical to many as it is irresistible to others, that
the Democrats will win a statewide race in Texas for the first time in 32
years. According to the latest New York Times/Siena University poll of the
race for U.S. Senate, James Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator seen
by national Democrats as one of the breakout stars of this cycle, is ahead
of his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney
general, by six points. The poll was conducted from Sept. 21 to Sept. 30.
A survey from mid-September, the ReconMR/Siena Research Institute poll,
also showed the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Gina Hinojosa, four
points ahead of the three-term G.O.P. incumbent, Greg Abbott, the most
dominant political figure in Texas. Cue the fluttering heartbeats. Cue, as
well, the eye-rolls. Given how thoroughly Republicans have dominated the
state, and how the hopes of Democrats have repeatedly crashed, some Texas
pollsters remain skeptical. “At some point, you do get conditioned by all
that’s happened in the past,” said James Henson, the director of the
University of Texas at Austin’s Texas Politics Project. “I mean, you look
at the trends and you have to admit that something’s going on. But you
still don’t want to believe your lying eyes, because you’ve been burned
for so long.” Mr. Henson was referring to the perennial spectacle of
much-ballyhooed Texas Democratic aspirants face-planting against the Lone
Star State’s red wall. First came Tony Sanchez Jr., the swaggering and
self-funding Laredo oilman whom Gov. Rick Perry dispatched in 2002 by an
18-point margin. Next was the state senator Wendy Davis, who attracted
worldwide attention for her filibuster in the Texas Legislature against an
anti-abortion measure but whom Mr. Abbott demolished by 20 points in 2014.
Finally, the El Paso congressman Beto O’Rourke came up 2.6 points short of
defeating Senator Ted Cruz in 2018 but then suffered a 10-point loss to
Mr. Abbott four years later. Even with the awareness of such humiliations,
Democrats find themselves maintaining that 2026 could, at long last, be
the year. President Trump’s deep unpopularity and the prospect of a blue
wave could, they insist, extend into the state he won by nearly 14 points
in 2024. According to a September survey conducted by Texas Southern
University, Mr. Trump is seven points underwater in Texas. Mr. Talarico
has run an energetic and well-financed campaign, while Mr. Paxton has
staged far fewer public events and has had to rely on outside groups to
fund an attack-ad blitzkrieg against his Democratic opponent. Mr. Abbott,
meanwhile, has outspent Ms. Hinojosa by a 10-to-one ratio, yet has been
unable to build an insurmountable lead. “People have vastly underestimated
Gina,” said Ms. Davis, now a political consultant and a senior adviser to
Planned Parenthood Texas Votes, an advocacy organization. “Dollar for
dollar, she’s running the best statewide campaign we’ve ever seen.” Such
optimism stands in defiance of the political axiom that Texas is where
idealistic Democrats go to be mugged by reality. The party’s demise there
is not a product of ill fortune, Mr. Henson said. “Governor Abbott has
built an impressive election machine that has benefited state-level
Republicans again and again for a decade and a half,” he said. “And the
Democratic machinery here is almost nonexistent.” A ‘Hollowing-Out’ I have
written about the politics of my native state at regular intervals for
more than three decades. After watching the Democrats’ century-long rule
in Texas come to a decisive end with Gov. Ann Richards’s loss to George W.
Bush in 1994, I saw the party descend into atrophy in which failure begot
more failure. “The 30-year drought has done a lot of things,” said Luke
Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party and the
founder of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund. “It’s kept donors on
the sidelines, which makes a lot of potentially good candidates not run
because there’s no belief they can win. And it also makes a lot of really
talented staff leave to find better-paying work in true battleground
states.” The Democratic Party has no counterpart to Mr. Abbott, and hasn’t
since 1993, when Senator Lloyd Bentsen moved to Washington to join
President Bill Clinton’s cabinet. Its weaknesses are even more glaring
farther down the hierarchy. In recent elections, as many as one-third of
state races have gone uncontested by Democrats. One-fifth of the party’s
county chairs and two-thirds of its precinct chairs have been left
unfilled. Until last year, the state party had a negative operating
budget. As the veteran Democratic consultant Matt Angle observed, “There’s
been a hollowing-out of the party.” Still, those of us who recall the
satisfied sense of invincibility among Texas Democrats after roughly a
century of one-party rule have detected similar signs of overconfidence
among the state’s ruling party. The party’s rightward tilt, increasingly
forceful with each legislative session, reached its apotheosis in March,
with Mr. Paxton’s primary victory over the more moderate Republican
four-term incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. Mr. Paxton, a close ally of Mr.
Trump’s, was impeached by the Republican-controlled State House (and later
acquitted by the State Senate) in 2023 over allegations that included
bribery. He was also accused by his wife of adultery. Mr. Trump endorsed
him anyway, all but guaranteeing his landslide primary triumph over Mr.
Cornyn but in the process testing the allegiance of center-right Texans.
In similar fashion, the Texas G.O.P. is in danger of losing many Latino
voters who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after years of siding with
Democrats. “We adopted a lazy way of campaigning that bit us on the ass,
and we’ve learned from that,” Mr. O’Rourke said. “Now it’s the Republicans
who’ve gotten really lazy and complacent and comfortable.” Signs of
Republican Overreach Simply spending one week driving through the vastness
of Texas, as I did in September, is all it takes to appreciate an underdog
party’s uphill battle. The state’s 32 million residents are spread across
20 media markets, many of them distinct ecosystems, from the urban colossi
of Houston and the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex to the oil patch of the
Texas Panhandle to the Latino-dominated borderlands of the Rio Grande
Valley. “When national donors are deciding where to invest, they look at a
place like Iowa, where $5 million can fully fund a race,” said Katherine
Fischer, the director of the Texas Majority PAC, which was established by
the liberal philanthropist Soros family. “That’s why Texas is always at
the bottom of their list. It’s just so damned big.” Reaching so many
markets presents a daunting challenge for an upstart candidate like Ms.
Hinojosa, a state representative from the border city of Brownsville.
“There’s still 20 percent of the electorate that doesn’t know who I am,”
she said in an interview in mid-September. To date, Ms. Hinojosa’s
campaign has said that it has raised about $20 million. For his part, Mr.
Talarico spent about $30 million earlier this year to introduce himself
statewide as a man of Christian faith and a member of the Texas House with
a record of supporting bipartisan legislation. Since that time, however,
Mr. Paxton and his associates have invested more than $100 million in an
effort to redefine his opponent as “radical” and “weird,” with ads that
quote from remarks Mr. Talarico made several years ago (and later
renounced) suggesting that “God is nonbinary” and that there are six
biological sexes. Mr. Paxton and his allies have at times questioned Mr.
Talarico’s manhood and even his Christianity, an effort to jolt the
sensibilities of a state prone to mythologizing godly and masculine
archetypes. “How they’re negatively defining Talarico is kind of a
bank-shot way of saying that he’s not a true Texas conservative,” Mr.
Henson said. Whether money can overwhelm conditions on the ground is the
riddle looming over the Texas races. In the border city of Laredo, which
Mr. Trump won in 2024 — the first time a Republican had done so in over a
century — signs of buyer’s remorse are evident. Arrests by Immigration and
Customs Enforcement agents in Laredo were higher in July than in any other
American city. Mr. Trump’s erratic trade policies have further created
instability at the city’s port of entry. While acknowledging the economic
concerns that many border residents share, Adrian Zapata, a business
executive in the health industry who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said in
an interview that the negative ads against Mr. Talarico were resonating
with some of his family members. “They see Talarico as an ultraliberal,”
he said. “They’re done with the ‘they/them.’ They’re going to vote for
Paxton just because of that.” As for Mr. Zapata, “I’m not ready to vote
for Talarico,” he said. “But I don’t like Paxton. He’s never done anything
for South Texas, and his personal and business dealings have hurt him a
lot with folks down here.” There is a similarly muddled electoral picture
in the cattle country of deep West Texas adjacent to Big Bend National
Park. Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott have aggressively championed a border wall
and artificial intelligence data centers, both of which threaten to
disrupt the region’s pastoral ethos. A coalition of more than 200
landowners has sued the federal government over the border wall, while
other residents have circulated a petition to protest the construction of
a new data center near Fort Stockton. George Johnson, a cattle feed
operator in Alpine, waved off such concerns, saying: “Folks worrying about
data centers were also worried when the internet got started. It’s
Talarico who scares me to death, him and all that socialist talk.” Others
in this largely conservative region harbor the view that Republicans have
failed to make good on their promises. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican
sheriff of Terrell County, said that both he and his county had voted for
Mr. Trump in 2024, but added, “Everything he campaigned on, we’re seeing
the opposite of, like going to war.” Sheriff Cleveland predicted that the
negative campaign ads by the Republicans would not factor as significantly
into the votes of his neighbors as “the price of groceries and gas, which
are compounded here because we’re so far from everywhere else.” But it is
in purple Tarrant County, dominated by Fort Worth, where the party could
pay the price for having potentially overestimated its mandate from the
voters. Conservative leaders have cut funds for nonprofits that aid
at-risk children, subjected school library books to right-wing litmus
tests and eliminated free bus rides to polling stations in poor
neighborhoods. “The far-right leaders here have implemented Project 2025
on a county level,” said Alisa Simmons, a Democrat and county commissioner
who is running to unseat the conservative county judge, Tim O’Hare. In an
early sign this year that area Republicans may be out of step with Tarrant
County’s constituents, a Democratic aviation machinist and union leader,
Taylor Rehmet, defeated Leigh Wambsganss, a well-funded Republican
Christian activist who led the conservative takeover of several metroplex
school boards. He won by 14 points in a January special election for a
State Senate seat covering a region that Mr. Trump won by 17 points in
2024. A ‘Gradualist’ Theory Which party prevails in Texas is a complicated
riddle. Historically a low-turnout state — it ranked second to last in the
2024 election, ahead of only Arkansas — Texas held a primary in March that
saw nearly one in four voters showing up to the polls, a modern record for
midterm participation, with Democrats slightly outpacing Republicans. A
few factors could conspire to thwart a blue wave in Texas. As of 2020,
straight-ticket voting is no longer possible in the state, which could
impact the mostly Democratic urban counties where that practice has
frequently been used by voters in past elections. Texas is one of only
eight states that lack universal online registration, while voting by mail
is also highly restricted. In January, Mr. Abbott turned over the state’s
list of approximately 18.7 million registered voters to the Trump
administration, and 1.2 million of them have subsequently been put on the
“suspense list” because their addresses have not been verified. The recent
shuttering of nearly one-third of Tarrant County’s polling sites by its
Republican-controlled county commission is particularly worrisome for
Democrats. “The reason we’ve lost these statewide races in the past is
because we’ve never gotten enough out of Tarrant County to overcome the
margins in rural Texas,” Ms. Davis said of the turnout. “If we don’t get
it to 53 or 54 percent this November, it’s game over. James and Gina can’t
win.” But the state’s Republicans have reasons of their own to be fretful.
Partly because of the recruitment efforts of the Texas Majority PAC and
Blueprint Texas, a down-ballot candidate support organization co-founded
by Ms. Davis earlier this year, the Democrats are fielding a full slate in
all 150 state races for the first time in a half-century. Though many of
these aspirants face long odds, their presence on the ballot could
energize the Democrats in predominantly conservative regions who have not
bothered to turn out in the past. “If we win on Nov. 3, most of those
names running down-ballot in really tough areas like East Texas and the
Hill Country and the Panhandle will be responsible,” Mr. O’Rourke said.
Mr. Henson added that while he remained skeptical about Democratic
enthusiasm being sufficient to carry the day for Mr. Talarico, he also
doubted that a last-minute avalanche of negative ads would prove decisive
for Mr. Paxton. “At a certain point, there’s diminishing impact once you
get past an absurd level of spending,” he said. Rather than project a
winner in November, Mr. Henson said he felt more comfortable embracing a
“gradualist” theory, one in which Texas does not become blue overnight,
but instead competitive. “Even if Talarico loses by a Beto-like margin,”
he said, “the next cycle is a presidential election, where Trump likely
won’t be popular and Democratic turnout will be higher. So there are
reasons for Texas Democrats to be optimistic.”'

name: Gina Hinojosa
body:
We turned a long shot into a dead heat. Now we need to finish it. | | | | I want to be straight with you, because you’ve earned that.

Back in April, I was down almost 7 points to Greg Abbott in the polling average. Political insiders wrote this race off. Then you showed up: you chipped in, spread the word, and proved that people all over the country believe Texas can be taken back. By October 7, we had cut that gap to just 1.3 points.

I know a lot of you saw that number and felt what I felt: we can actually do this.

But since then, the polls have moved in the wrong direction. Today, the average has me trailing Abbott by 2.7 points.

Here’s what I need you to hear: 2.7 points is not a lost race. This is one of the most competitive governor’s races in the country, and it will be decided by turnout, by organizing, and by what we do in these final days.

**That’s the first step. The goal is getting Medicare out of the picture.** Instead of the guaranteed coverage you paid into your whole working life, you’d get a voucher and be sent off to shop among private insurance plans. So who wins? Insurance companies will get billions in taxpayer dollars flowing to them. They'll get to decide what’s covered, what’s denied, and what you pay out of pocket. Meanwhile, you, me, and every American who used to enjoy the guaranteed coverage we've earned from Medicare**—** we'll all lose, a lot. **Medicare works because it’s a promise. Michael Alfonso wants to break that promise and hand even more health care decisions over to corporations.** People all across the Northwoods count on that promise: retired loggers, teachers, farmers, small business owners. They earned their Medicare. Fred Clark will fight to protect it, lower prescription costs, and keep care within reach for rural communities, not turn it into a profit center for insurers. We have one week left, and Alfonso has a lot of outside money behind him. Our TV ad is how voters across this district hear the truth before they vote. clean_body: Caught red-handed| | | Peter, Michael Alfonso was caught on tape saying he wants to privatize Medicare. Here’s what he said in River Falls. He was asked whether the voucher model Republicans use for private school tuition could work for health care. His answer: that’s his “entire approach.” = That’s the first step. The goal is getting Medicare out of the picture. Instead of the guaranteed coverage you paid into your whole working life, you’d get a voucher and be sent off to shop among private insurance plans. So who wins? Insurance companies will get billions in taxpayer dollars flowing to them. They'll get to decide what’s covered, what’s denied, and what you pay out of pocket. Meanwhile, you, me, and every American who used to enjoy the guaranteed coverage we've earned from Medicare— we'll all lose, a lot. Medicare works because it’s a promise. Michael Alfonso wants to break that promise and hand even more health care decisions over to corporations. People all across the Northwoods count on that promise: retired loggers, teachers, farmers, small business owners. They earned their Medicare. Fred Clark will fight to protect it, lower prescription costs, and keep care within reach for rural communities, not turn it into a profit center for insurers. We have one week left, and Alfonso has a lot of outside money behind him. Our TV ad is how voters across this district hear the truth before they vote. Hey folks,
Donald Trump says Russia has been "fine" in Ukraine. Mitch McConnell, of all people, is now publicly calling him out for it.
Yes, you read that correctly. McConnell has largely disappeared from public view, but an op-ed under his name is suddenly delivering one of the sharpest Republican rebukes of Trump's treatment of Vladimir Putin. This whole thing is bizarre, and incredibly revealing.
* [**00:01:07**] Mitch McConnell reemerges with a scathing op-ed attacking Trump's handling of Putin and Ukraine, despite barely being seen publicly in weeks.
* [**00:03:16**] McConnell's message is blunt: coddling Putin won't bring peace. We get into why Trump's continued accommodation of Russia should alarm everyone.
* [**00:05:57**] Trump says Russia has been "fine" in Ukraine while attacks continue, raising an obvious question: where are all the other Republicans supposedly committed to standing with Ukraine?
* [**00:08:04**] We follow the money as Trump touts energy moves involving Russia, and I explain why I think his approach does nothing meaningful for Americans while potentially benefiting Putin.
* [**00:10:18**] With the midterms about a week away, we get to the bigger political question: will a Republican defeat finally convince anyone in Trump's party to stand up to him?

This episode is about Ukraine, Putin, Trump, and the staggering cowardice inside today's Republican Party. I have plenty of problems with Mitch McConnell, but if an op-ed under his name is one of the only Republican voices willing to challenge Trump over Russia, that tells us just how broken this party has become. **If you value independent media willing to keep asking where the hell the accountability is, help me keep doing this work.**

body:
Our TV deadline is tomorrow night.
# [](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)[](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)
Peter,
**We only have until tomorrow night to add more TV ads in Texas.** [**If that’s all you need to hear, chip in $5 or any amount right now to help us reach more voters in the final stretch.**](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/625?c0=em_ms_gh_20261028_2_ads.a4WJEt&refcode=em20261028-2569&amount=5&t=1&akid=2569%2E299639%2E8mMF5c)
[****](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/625?c0=em_ms_gh_20261028_2_ads.a4WJEt&refcode=em20261028-2569&amount=5&t=2&akid=2569%2E299639%2E8mMF5c)
Early voting is happening right now, and this is when most Texans cast their ballots. By the time early voting ends on Friday, the majority of votes in this race could already be in.
_**That means the voters we reach this week are the voters who will decide this election.**_
Here’s how the deadline works: TV stations need our final order on Friday to secure airtime for the rest of the race. That means our TV budget will be whatever we’ve raised by **tomorrow night**. Whatever we have in hand by then decides how many undecided voters see our ads before they head to the polls.
And in a state as big as Texas, TV is how we reach the voters other tools can’t. It reaches rural counties where houses are miles apart, and it’s hard to knock every door. It reaches voters who don’t spend their evenings scrolling social media. And Spanish-language TV lets us talk directly to Latino voters from the Valley to El Paso, the voters Greg Abbott has taken for granted and who could decide this race.
After tomorrow, every dollar we raise will still go to work reaching voters and turning them out through Election Day. But tomorrow is our last chance to add more TV to our plan.
**We didn’t set these deadlines, but we have to meet them**. How many voters we reach before they cast their ballots depends on what we raise today.
**[So I’m turning to you, Peter. Will you chip in $5 or any amount right now to help us expand our TV buy before tomorrow’s deadline?](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/625?c0=em_ms_gh_20261028_2_ads.a4WJEt&refcode=em20261028-2569&amount=5&t=3&akid=2569%2E299639%2E8mMF5c)**

Thank you,
Gina
